Often seen instead: quotes or copies the evidence without explaining its significance.
BEFORE YOU ANSWER

What is it really asking? Find the command word first. This practice question carries no marks, so size the answer from its join (explain, argue, compare or judge (extended answer)). In an exam, the marks tell you how far to go.
Use the case. Every point should name something from it. A true fact that ignores the case can score nothing.
Don’t hand the question back. Repeating its wording, or copying labels from the source, is not an answer.

shots.text:
JOIN IT UP

Complete what this question requires: no more reasoning than it asks for, and no less precision.

Explain, argue, compare or judge (extended answer)

Refused without it: relevant points with no reasoning between them, or not applied to the case.

“a well-developed line of reasoning which is clear and logically structured”
OCR GCSE J277/01, June 2023, Q6, band 3

Where answers stopped at one point, the step that broke was reasoning in 39 of 68 examiner findings, against 12 of 119 at other levels; and answers stop short in 32% of question parts whose scheme requires reasons, against 6% where it does not. Where reasons are required, the fix is the link, not more facts. A synthesis to test (hypothesis 10), model-read, not yet checked by a teacher. Why this join.

shots.title: Transfer check
shots.text:
TRANSFER CHECK
NEAR: THE SAME LINK, A NEW CASE
“A phone advert says: ‘108 MP camera. Every detail, captured.’ Choose your abstraction: the most revealing line, or what isn’t there. Weigh both routes.”
FAR: THE SAME PRINCIPLE, SOMEWHERE ELSE
“From two sources on the same historical event, choose the one line that best supports your argument, and say why you rejected the other.” This tests choosing evidence by purpose, not this advert.

Score both on the same SOLO scale as the stage. Ideally set after a delay and without support. If one fails, check the new topic’s knowledge first: a failure may be missing knowledge, not the answering skill. Drafted items, not yet tried with students.

shots.title: Answer routine
shots.text:
ANSWER ROUTINE
31% of coded examiner-report findings describe wrong ideas. Each step is meant to guard against one kind of mistake: a design to test.
1. Decode
24%
Find the command word. Size the answer from the question; in an exam, the marks say how far to go. Every point must use the case.
Guards against exam technique, not applied to the scenario, misusing the information given.
2. Retrieve
46%
Bring: Connotation, Omission, Performance factors.
Guards against misconceptions, found difficult.
3. Reason
7%
One route that earns the link: Two possible routes → what each would reveal → a choice made by which gives stronger evidence for the question.
Guards against stopped short.
4. Refine
8%
Use technical terms where accuracy depends on them; keep the rest clear and natural.
Guards against imprecise wording.
5. Review
14%
Re-read the question: does the answer do everything it asks?
Guards against slips and calculation errors.
After marking, log each lost mark by the step that failed. A design to try, not a tested result: the routine and its evidence.

THE MENTAL OPERATIONS THIS QUESTION NEEDS

Operations you move between, not steps in a fixed order: you might go back to retrieve after interpreting the question, or rebuild a connection after checking.

Interpret

Choose one route: the most revealing line, or what is missing.
Connect
Link the choice to the question it will help answer.
Teaching method from the research, not specific to this question · lever 1: writing explanations as cause linked to effect

State the choice, then why it is the stronger evidence.
Check
Is the choice something the next stage can use?

shots.title: Fluency practice
shots.text:
FLUENCY PRACTICE

Practice for when you can already do it accurately: the aim now is quick and smooth.

A GOOD ANSWER
Correct without hesitation, with few prompts.
PRACTISE BY
Short, regular, timed repetition. Cut the prompts as you improve.
TO REACH GENERALISATION
Try it on a different case from the one you practised. That is generalisation.
Stages of mastery from the instructional hierarchy (Haring and Eaton, 1978). Draft: each stage’s placement is judged from its power words, not from examiner data. Draft guidance written for this app.

shots.title: The missing-link ladder
shots.text:
THE MISSING-LINK LADDER
The link to build: Two possible routes → what each would reveal → a choice made by which gives stronger evidence for the question
1. Independent
Choose your abstraction: the single most revealing line, or what isn't there.
2. Neutral prompt
“How did you decide between the two routes?”
3. Partial hint
“Which route gives you something you could use as evidence for your question?”
4. Model
Show the worked example (Student C on the Question tab), then withdraw it.
5. New task: independent (no hints), but asked
“A phone advert says: ‘108 MP camera. Every detail, captured.’ Choose your abstraction: the most revealing line, or what isn’t there. Weigh both routes.”
Repair, unprompted, in a later and different task: In a later analysis, gives the reason for a choice of abstraction in terms of what it lets them argue, without being asked why. 
Rung 5 shows independent performance when asked; later independent use, unprompted, gives stronger evidence of learning. If rung 5 fails, check the new topic’s knowledge first.

shots.title: What kind of mark scheme this is
shots.text:
The examiner-report research is computer science only. Critical text analysis has no reports of its own, so these findings come from computer science papers and are not yet known for this subject.
WHAT KIND OF MARK SCHEME THIS IS

NOT EXAMINED This framework is not examined, so it has no mark scheme of its own. Anything below is borrowed from the closest examined stage, and says so.
No demand check here: the demand audit covers six command words (Identify, Complete, Describe, State, Give and Explain).
Closest examined stage: Computer Science (GCSE), command word 11, Justify. Choosing a route and saying why is a Justify: the choice, then the reasons that fit it. This framework is not examined, so the evidence below is that stage’s.

shots.title: How the marks are awarded
shots.text:
HOW THE MARKS ARE AWARDED
3 marks
The choice (1), then two reasons, or a reason and its follow-on.
OCR J277/01, June 2023, Q3(c)(i), compression for a text file: lossless (1); no data is removed (1) … and a text file needs every character to work (1).
4 marks
In OCR 2024 and 2025 the choice earns nothing: all 4 marks are for reasons that fit it, each linked to the user.
OCR J277/01, June 2024, Q5(b)(i), storage for a musician: solid state is robust (1) … which matters if the device is moved (1), and so on.

NOT CREDITED

Reasons that do not match the choice made.
Comparisons with no object: “faster”, without saying faster at what.
Reading a mark scheme

shots.title: What examiners saw
shots.text:
WHAT EXAMINERS SAW

OCR J277/01, June 2024, Q5(b)(i): magnetic or solid state storage for a musician

WEAKER ANSWERS

“Solid state is faster”, without saying faster at what.

STRONGER ANSWERS

Links each property to the user: solid state is robust, which matters because the musician may move the device.

Paraphrased from the examiners’ report for that paper.

shots.title: What the mark schemes show
shots.text:
WHAT THE MARK SCHEMES SHOW

Partly consistent with this level

The marks reward reasons linked to the context (relational). The judgement is required, but earns at most 1 mark on its own.

IN THE PAPERS
8 question parts, 2–4 marks
HOW MARKS ARE EARNED
The choice earns 1 mark in some papers and none in others. The rest of the marks are for reasons that match the choice, with follow-on marks for linking each one to the context.

The most-used command words are not on this ladder: State (49 parts), Identify (37), Shade (29), Write (26), Give (24) and Tick (21), about half of all parts. They are marked as one fact or several separate points, so they sit with Define and Describe.

Read from the 368 question parts that have a mark scheme, of 384 in 12 GCSE Computer Science papers (AQA 8525 June 2022–23, OCR J277 June 2022–25; 16 OCR J277/02 parts have none in this set), with their examiners’ reports. Readings by this app, not yet checked by a teacher.

shots.title: Marks and substance, across every command word
shots.text:
MARKS AND SUBSTANCE, ACROSS EVERY COMMAND WORD
The command word signals the kind of response; the content and the context decide the thinking it takes. The marks show how much substance is wanted: up to 5 marks, count roughly one unit of substance per mark, as a planning aid that the actual mark scheme overrides. At 6 marks or more, 7 of the 32 parts are levels-marked and judged as a whole; the other 25 stay points-marked.
Marks	What it needs	How the marks fall
1
115 parts
	One precise point.	
The exact term or fact: “cache size”, not “cache”.
Mostly State, Shade, Give, Identify and Define.
2
111 parts
	Two points, or one point and its expansion.	
Define: what it is, and what sets it apart.
“Describe one …” or “Explain one …”: the point, then how or why.
3
51 parts
	Three units of substance.	
Three separate points (“State three …”).
A name or choice, then two points describing or justifying it.
A three-step chain or process.
4
49 parts
	Four units, usually in pairs.	
Two points, each expanded or applied to the scenario (2 + 2).
A choice and three reasons, or four reasons with no mark for the choice.
Four steps in order, or four table rows.

shots.title: Marks and substance, across every command word (continued)
shots.text:
5
10 parts
	Mostly building: completing code or a table, one mark per element.	
Each correct element earns its own mark.
6+
32 parts
	Two different kinds of question, and most are still points-marked.	
Write an algorithm (13 of the 32): one mark for each required feature, such as the inputs, the decision, the loop and each output.
Discuss (7 of the 32, 6–9 marks, levels-marked): the whole answer is judged for coverage, application to the scenario, balance and structure. The papers' eighth levels-marked part is a 4-mark Explain.
The other 12 are points-marked: one mark per creditable point.
Counted from the 368 question parts with a mark scheme, of 384 in the same 12 papers, whatever their command word. Each count says what it includes. Readings by this app, not yet checked by a teacher.
